The AI Transformation Practice 
UC San Diego's capability for end-to-end transformation of institutional 
services, delivered by OSI 
Draft · June 12 2026 
 
What this is 
The AI Transformation Practice is a campus capability for redesigning whole 
institutional service lifecycles rather than individual tasks or tools. It brings to UC San 
Diego three disciplines the university does not currently have in any meaningful 
institutional form: service design, which maps how a service actually works from end 
to end; AI opportunity analysis, which identifies where intelligence can augment, 
automate, or reimagine specific moments in that service; and AI governance, which 
ensures every AI decision point operates within published university standards for 
ethics, privacy, security, and human judgment. Founding the practice means building all 
three and joining them in one method. 
The practice is housed in OSI (Operational Strategic Initiatives) and delivered by its 
consultants. It is designed at the campus level, against campus-wide standards, so that 
any unit at the university can request a transformation engagement and know what it 
will get: the same method, the same guardrails, the same quality bar. 
The practice also carries a founding obligation beyond its engagements. The university 
does not yet have an agreed definition of return on investment for AI, or an 
executive-level set of metrics for measuring AI's impact across the institution. Building 
that measurement framework is part of the practice's mandate. Without it, the 
practice could transform services but could not show the university what the 
transformation was worth. 
The problem it solves 
Most AI adoption at universities happens at the level of the tool. A unit buys or builds 
something, points it at a task, and measures whether the task got faster. This produces 

scattered wins and a growing list of unmanaged risks, because nobody is looking at the 
service the task belongs to. A faster step in a broken process leaves the process broken. 
The alternative is to start with the service lifecycle: the full journey a service takes from 
beginning to end, with every touchpoint, handoff, and decision point made visible. Once 
the lifecycle is mapped, AI opportunities stop being guesses and become design choices, 
each one tied to a specific moment, a specific value, and a specific guardrail. This is the 
work of service design, and it is why the practice's method comes from that discipline 
rather than from technology procurement. 
The method: three layers 
Every engagement applies the same three-layer model to a chosen institutional service 
lifecycle. 
Layer 1 is the lifecycle map. OSI consultants, working with the unit that owns the 
service and the people who run it day to day, document the end-to-end journey: stages, 
touchpoints, handoffs, decision points, and pain signals. The tools here are the 
established ones of service design: journey mapping, service blueprinting, stakeholder 
interviews, process documentation. Nothing in this layer explicitly involves AI. It exists 
so that the layers above it rest on how the service actually works rather than on how the 
org chart says it works. 
Layer 2 is the AI opportunity layer. Against the map, the team, including ITS, 
identifies where AI can augment, automate, or reimagine specific lifecycle moments. 
Every opportunity is tagged by the kind of value it creates: efficiency gain, experience 
lift, risk reduction, or retention and outcome impact. Every opportunity also carries an 
impact hypothesis, stated before anything is built and expressed in the campus 
measurement framework described below, so the engagement can later be judged 
against what it promised.  
Layer 3 is the governance and ethics layer. Governance in this practice works 
through published standards rather than a review gate. The campus maintains a set of 
high-level AI guidelines and guardrails, grounded in the UC Responsible AI Principles, 
that are reviewed, evaluated, and refreshed on a regular cadence, likely quarterly. These 
guardrails are published openly, embedded in policies and procedures, and, where the 
work is technical, enforced in infrastructure: ITS protocols and agent instruction files 
that put the standards directly into the development environment, so conformance is 
built in from the start. 

In an engagement, Layer 3 means designing within the published guardrails. Every AI 
decision point in the blueprint is mapped to the standards it must meet: where human 
judgment is required, how data is handled (federated by default, no raw institutional 
data in models, architecture aligned with ITS), and which guardrails govern its 
operation. The standing rule from the pilot applies across the practice: AI drafts, flags, 
and synthesizes; humans decide, always. 
When an engagement encounters a situation the published guardrails do not cover, the 
gap is documented and fed into the next quarterly refresh. This is deliberate. The 
guardrails improve through contact with real lifecycles, and each engagement helps the 
institution find the edges of its current standards. 
The three layers are a standing structure, not phases that finish and disappear. A 
transformed lifecycle keeps its map current, keeps its impact commitments measured, 
and keeps its conformance to the guardrails as both the lifecycle and the standards 
evolve. 
How an engagement works 
A transformation engagement moves through four stages. 
Selection. Units request engagements through a single intake process. Requests are 
prioritized against explicit criteria: readiness of the owning unit, risk profile of the 
lifecycle, expected value, and fit with campus strategy. Not every request becomes an 
engagement, and the criteria are public so units can see why. 
Mapping. The Layer 1 work, led by OSI consultants in partnership with the lifecycle 
owner and the business owners who hold the working knowledge of the service. This 
stage ends with a validated lifecycle map and an honest account of the service pain 
points. 
Design. Layers 2 and 3 together: opportunities identified and tagged, impact 
hypotheses stated, every decision point mapped to the published guardrails, and any 
gaps in the guardrails documented for the refresh cycle. This stage ends with a 
transformation blueprint that the unit's leadership signs, including what will be 
measured and who is accountable for it. 
Implementation and transfer. Build happens on ITS infrastructure using the 
TritonAI harness against the Data Insights & Analytics blueprint and within the 
guardrails embedded in the Citizen Developer framework. The engagement ends with 

the capability living in the unit and the measurement living on the executive dashboard, 
without an ongoing dependency on the consulting team. 
Measuring what transformation does 
The practice's measurement work has two jobs, and they are different in kind. 
The first job is to give the university a working definition of AI ROI and an executive 
metrics layer. Neither exists today, and the most recent budget cycle made the cost of 
that absence visible: initiatives that could not be compared, impact claims that could not 
be evaluated, and executive conversations about AI investment conducted without 
shared numbers. The practice builds this framework as a founding deliverable, in 
partnership with the executives who will use it, and every engagement's impact 
hypotheses are expressed in its terms. The definition of ROI needs to be broad enough 
to be honest: direct efficiency and cost measures where they apply, and experience, risk, 
and institutional-capability measures where the value is real but does not appear as a 
line item. 
The second job is harder: measuring movement toward a future state that cannot yet be 
fully specified. Destination metrics work when the destination is known. Wholesale 
transformation, by definition, includes outcomes the institution has not yet imagined, 
and a measurement system built only on fixed KPIs will either miss those outcomes or 
discourage them. So the framework carries two kinds of measures. Destination 
measures track progress against what an engagement explicitly promised: the impact 
hypotheses, the baseline KPIs, the dashboard numbers. Adaptive-capacity measures 
track whether the institution is becoming more able to evolve: how quickly units absorb 
and extend transformed lifecycles, how often guardrail gaps are found and closed, how 
much of the next engagement a unit can run without the consulting team, and what new 
options each transformation opens that did not exist before it. 
Both kinds of measures are re-baselined on the same quarterly cadence as the 
guardrails, so that as the future state comes into view, the metrics move with it. One 
institutional rhythm governs both what we permit and how we know it is working. 
The existing four-dimension impact framework (operational capacity, institutional 
readiness, risk reduction, system-level influence) is the starting scaffold for the 
executive layer, and it maps cleanly onto both kinds of measures. It is a starting point 
for the measurement work to test and extend, though, and should not be treated as the 
finished answer. 

Roles 
The unit head (lifecycle owner). Owns the service and the outcome. Provides the 
business owners who hold the working knowledge. Signs the blueprint and is 
accountable for the impact commitments in it. 
OSI consultants. Deliver the engagement. Every engagement has three leads, drawn 
from the consulting team: one for the service map, one for AI opportunities, and one for 
governance and ethics. These are roles on an engagement, not job titles, and consultants 
are expected to work across all three over time. The team brings OSI's existing depth in 
Lean Six Sigma and PROSCI change management into the transformation method 
rather than running it alongside.  
The Director of AI Strategy. Designs the practice: the method, the intake logic, the 
quality standards, the measurement framework, and the governance interfaces. Trains 
and coaches the consulting clusters through the pilot, then moves to milestone-level 
review of engagements. Does not deliver engagements. 
The AI Engagement function. Owns the guardrail lifecycle: establishes the 
high-level guidelines and guardrails, publishes them, embeds them in policy and 
procedure, and runs the quarterly review and refresh, incorporating the gaps that 
engagements surface. No per-use-case or per-engagement approval sits here; the 
function maintains standards that everyone designs within. 
ITS. Technical architecture, including the federated data model that is the practice's 
default, and the enforcement layer: the protocols and agent instruction files that embed 
the published guardrails directly in the development environment. 
Data Insights & Analytics. Data architecture and the migration path from activity 
hubs to the federated model. 
Chancellor and executives. Hold the practice accountable through the executive 
metrics layer and set the strategic direction for which lifecycles matter most. 
The pilot: the HR employee lifecycle 
The practice proves itself on the HR employee lifecycle, in partnership with the CHRO, 
beginning with the performance appraisal sub-process. The choice is deliberate. 
Performance appraisal is the lifecycle stage with the lowest risk profile and the highest 

readiness in the owning unit, and it is a process whose pain is widely felt, which makes 
improvement visible and credible. 
The pilot exercises all three layers on a real service. The appraisal journey is mapped 
from goal setting through formal review. AI opportunities are identified in goal 
alignment, sentiment analysis, bias detection, and review synthesis, each with a stated 
impact hypothesis. And the governance model is proven in a demanding domain, 
because employee-facing AI is exactly where published guardrails have to show they can 
carry weight without case-by-case review. The pilot's blueprint maps every decision 
point to the published standards, documents every gap the standards do not yet cover, 
and holds the non-negotiables structurally: no rating is ever AI-generated, and humans 
decide, always. Baseline KPIs (completion rate, manager time per cycle, retention 
following review) are measured before anything ships, so the impact claims are tested 
against numbers that existed first. 
The pilot has two further purposes beyond the service itself. It is the training ground 
where OSI consultants learn the method by running it, with coaching, so the second 
engagement is theirs. And it is the first real test of the guardrail model and the 
measurement framework working together. If the published standards and the executive 
metrics can handle performance appraisal, they can handle most of what the campus 
will bring. 
What success looks like 
Success for a practice like this cannot be counted only in completed engagements, 
because transformation of a living institution does not complete. Services keep 
changing, the technology keeps changing, and the standards governing both refresh 
every quarter. So the practice needs two kinds of success criteria: near-term evidence 
that the model works, and a longer-term account of what the practice is doing to the 
institution's relationships and capabilities. 
In its first year, the practice is succeeding if the pilot delivers what its blueprint 
promised, if the consulting team can run the method with growing independence (the 
practice designer's role shifting from coaching toward milestone review, with the 
judgment retained to step in deeper when an engagement warrants it), if every AI 
decision point that runs through the practice conforms to published guardrails with 
documented data stewardship, and if the measurement framework is adopted at the 
executive level and used in real budget conversations rather than admired in a deck. 

The longer measure is what happens to the relationship between OSI and the units it 
works with. Transformation is not an event that an engagement performs on a service 
and then closes out. A transformed lifecycle is a living thing: the AI capabilities available 
to it change every quarter, the guardrails refresh, the measures re-baseline, and the 
service itself keeps evolving as the institution does. So success does not look like OSI 
finishing and leaving. It looks like the character of the partnership evolving. In the 
engagement, OSI does the work with the unit while building the unit's ability to own it. 
Afterward, the unit owns its lifecycle, and OSI remains a long-term partner in its 
evolution: there for the next layer of opportunity, the next stage of the lifecycle, the next 
thing the technology makes possible that nobody could have specified at the start. What 
should disappear over time is dependence. What should deepen over time is the 
partnership. 
That gives the practice two failure modes to watch, not one. The first is holding on too 
long: a backlog of units that cannot move without the consulting team, which means 
capability never actually transferred. The second is letting go completely: units that 
went through an engagement and then stalled, because the relationship ended when the 
project did and nobody was there for the evolutionary work. The measurement 
framework should make both visible early, and the adaptive-capacity measures exist 
largely for this purpose. 
There is also a final, more reflective test. A practice whose purpose is to help the 
institution evolve has to be able to evolve itself. A year from founding, the guardrails, the 
metrics, and the method should all look different from how they look today, changed by 
what the engagements taught everyone involved. If they are unchanged, the practice has 
been administering a process rather than learning from one. 
Operating principles 
Five commitments define how the practice works, in every engagement, without 
exception. 
1. The lifecycle is the unit of work. An engagement transforms a service from end to 
end; tools are one of the ways that happens, never the goal in themselves. 
2. Impact is hypothesized before build, measured after, and reported in the campus 
framework. No opportunity progresses without a claim it can be held to, in 
numbers the executives have agreed to use. 

3. Humans decide. AI drafts, flags, synthesizes, and suggests. Decisions about 
people, money, and ranking stay with people, and the guardrails enforce this 
structurally rather than leaving it to good intentions. 
4. Governance is published, embedded, and refreshed. Guardrails live in policy and 
in the development environment itself, improve quarterly from what 
engagements discover, and apply to everyone the same way. 
5. Capability transfers. The practice trains the people who will own the work, in the 
unit and in the consulting team, and gets out of the delivery path on schedule. 
Where this starts 
The practice does not need a long runway. The pilot partner is committed, the method is 
drawn, and the last budget cycle already established the appetite for what it measures. 
Three decisions put it in motion. 
Charter the design phase: one quarter to build the engagement model, the intake 
process, the first version of the measurement framework, and the guardrail structure, 
working with the AI Engagement function and ITS. Launch the pilot: the performance 
appraisal engagement with the CHRO, baselined before anything progresses, run as the 
proving ground for the method, the guardrails, and the metrics at once. And convene the 
executive measurement conversation early, because the framework only carries weight if 
the people it reports to helped define what it measures. 
From there, the work proceeds as this document describes it: one lifecycle at a time, 
within published standards, measured in numbers the institution agrees on. Parts of this 
model will turn out to be wrong, and the pilot exists to find out which ones while the 
cost of being wrong is still small. The design phase is where that learning starts. 

 
 
AI Council  

  
Operational Strategic Initiatives (OSI) proposes an inaugural UC San Diego AI Council 
to help faculty, staff, students, and researchers adopt AI responsibly. The Council will 
publish and maintain AI Principles, localized from the UCOP Responsible AI Principles, 
that guide individual AI use, enterprise-level agreements, and the AI Transformation 
Practice. It functions as an advisory and coordinating body rather than a regulatory 
authority: it has no sign-off, enforcement, or gatekeeping power, and accountability for 
AI use remains with the individual user. Its work spans four pillars: AI Standards 
(writing and updating the Principles), Communication Feed (informing TritonAI's 
website and newsletter, which serve as the campus communication hub), Literacy and 
Empowerment (signposting education gaps to TritonAI Learning), and AI Ethics and 
Compliance Consulting (advising on ethics and compliance questions at the individual 
and enterprise level). 
The Council operates as two connected tiers. A permanent Core Group, drawn from 
Privacy, IT, Legal, Ethics and Compliance, HR, and Data, carries out the Council's 
standing work on three-year staggered terms. A wider Full Council, spanning all Vice 
Chancellor areas plus one student seat, meets quarterly and self-selects into specific 
projects based on relevance. When an AI integration project reaches a stage where 
Council input is useful, a representative presents to the Council or a member embeds 
with the project team before implementation; the Core Group determines whether wider 
Council members are needed. Output takes the form of flagged issues and 
recommendations, not approval, and the Council cannot block a project's progression. 
No standing subgroups exist beyond the Core Group, though organic sub-groups may 
form independently and can channel feedback to the Council. 
The Council's reporting line remains an open decision for the Chancellor, with options 
including direct reporting, the Senate-Administration Council, Ethics and Compliance, 
or Cabinet. Year-one success will be measured by published AI Principles, optional 
department-level localization of those Principles, the Council becoming the campus's 
trusted first stop for AI ethics and compliance questions, and a baseline survey of 
campus AI attitudes and usage.
